text: American Express Company, a globally integrated payments company founded in 1850 and incorporated in 1965 as a New York corporation, operates as a bank holding company under the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956, as amended, and is subject to supervision and examination by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. The company provides credit and charge cards to consumers, small businesses, mid-sized companies, and large corporations worldwide through its various products and services, available via mobile and online applications, affiliate marketing, customer referral programs, third-party service providers, direct mail, telephone, in-house sales teams, and direct response advertising. Its businesses are organized into four reportable operating segments: U.S. Consumer Services (USCS), Commercial Services (CS), International Card Services (ICS), and Global Merchant and Network Services (GMNS), with corporate functions and certain other businesses included in Corporate & Other. The company’s end-to-end integrated payments platform connects Card Members and merchants through direct relationships, enabling access to spending data for risk underwriting, fraud reduction, and targeted marketing, while protecting data in compliance with applicable policies and laws. It also obtains data through contractual relationships with third-party card issuers, merchant acquirers, aggregators, and processors. The company’s global proprietary card-issuing businesses are conducted through USCS, CS, and ICS, offering a broad range of card products, rewards, and services to consumers and commercial customers, with a focus on attracting Millennial and Gen Z customers and expanding SME offerings through products like business checking and consumer rewards checking, as well as digital capabilities from acquisitions of Kabbage, Resy, and acompay. The ICS organization consolidates consumer, SME, and large commercial card issuing activities outside the U.S. to better serve local priorities, with significant billed business in the United Kingdom, European Union, Australia, Japan, Canada, and Mexico. For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022, worldwide billed business (spending on American Express cards issued by the company) was $1,338 billion, and the company had 76.7 million proprietary cards-in-force worldwide. The GMNS segment manages relationships with millions of merchants globally, including signing new merchants, setting discount rates, and handling merchant servicing, and operates through programs like OptBlue® that allow third-party acquirers to contract directly with small merchants. The company also provides fraud-prevention tools, marketing solutions, and data analytics to merchants and partners. Through its card network, American Express operates in approximately 103 countries and territories, licensing the American Express brand to third-party banks and institutions to issue local currency cards and serve as merchant acquirers. For the year ended December 31, 2022, worldwide network services processed volume (spending on American Express cards issued by third parties) was $214.5 billion, and the company had 56.5 million cards-in-force issued by third parties worldwide. The company’s diverse customer base includes consumers, small businesses, mid-sized companies, and large corporations, with a global footprint supported by partnerships. Key partners include Delta Air Lines, Marriott International, Hilton Worldwide Holdings, British Airways, Amazon.com (via Pay with Points), PayPal, i2c, BILL, BillTrust, Versapay, and Fine Hotels and Resorts. Delta is the company’s largest strategic partner, with the Delta cobrand portfolio representing approximately 10 percent of worldwide network volumes and about 21 percent of worldwide Card Member loans as of December 31, 2022. The Delta cobrand portfolio generates fee revenue and interest income from Card Members and discount revenue from Delta and other merchants for spending on Delta cobrand cards, with the current agreement running through the end of 2029 and the company planning significant investments in the partnership. Delta also participates in the Membership Rewards program, provides travel-related benefits such as airport lounge access, accepts American Express cards as a merchant, and serves as a corporate payments customer. The company’s spend-centric business model generates revenue primarily by driving spending on its cards and secondarily through finance charges and fees. As of June 30, 2022, the aggregate market value of the registrant’s voting shares held by non-affiliates was approximately $104.0 billion based on the closing sale price on the New York Stock Exchange. As of February 2, 2023, there were 744,192,702 common shares outstanding. The company is a well-known seasoned issuer and has filed all required reports under Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 during the preceding 12 months and has been subject to such filing requirements for the past 90 days. It has submitted electronically every Interactive Data File required under Rule 405 of Regulation S-T and is classified as a large accelerated filer. The registrant has filed a report on and attestation to its management’s assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting under Section 404(b) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. The terms “American Express,” “we,” “our,” or “us” refer to American Express Company and its subsidiaries on a consolidated basis unless otherwise stated or implied. The use of the term “partner” or “partnering” does not imply a formal legal partnership and does not alter the terms of American Express’ relationship with third parties.

Revenues and expenses related to Delta are significant and represent a major source of value for American Express Card Members. The Delta cobrand portfolio accounted for approximately 10 percent of worldwide network volumes and about 21 percent of worldwide Card Member loans as of December 31, 2022. This portfolio generates fee revenue and interest income from Card Members and discount revenue from Delta and other merchants for spending on Delta cobrand cards. The current Delta cobrand agreement extends through the end of 2029, and the company expects to continue making significant investments in this partnership. Delta is also a key participant in the Membership Rewards program, provides travel-related benefits and services including airport lounge access for certain American Express Card Members, accepts American Express cards as a merchant, and is a corporate payments customer. American Express works with all partners to deliver value, choice, and unique experiences to its customer base. The company’s “spend-centric” business model primarily generates revenue by driving spending on its cards and secondarily through finance charges and fees. Spending on American Express cards is, on average, higher per card than that of competitors, offering merchants loyal customers and larger transactions, which in turn enables the company to invest in attractive rewards, targeted marketing, and other programs for both Card Members and merchants. This model differentiates American Express cards and provides value to Card Members, merchants, and business partners. The American Express brand, known for trust, security, and service, is among the most valuable globally and is protected through extensive investment in trademarks, service marks, and patents worldwide. The company aims to deliver the world’s best customer experience daily, with its reputation for service recognized through numerous awards. Customer care professionals, travel consultants, and partners are trained to enhance the brand experience and deepen customer relationships. American Express focuses on four strategic imperatives: expanding leadership in the premium consumer space by offering benefits across everyday spending, borrowing, travel, and lifestyle needs, expanding global business partnerships, and creating experiences that attract high-spending customers; building on its strong position in commercial payments by evolving card value propositions, differentiating corporate card and accounts payable solutions, and introducing innovative financing, banking, and payment products for business customers; strengthening its global, integrated network by increasing merchant acceptance, providing fraud protection, marketing insights, and connections to high-spending Card Members, and collaborating with network partners to expand offerings; and leveraging its unique global position to support its other strategic goals. Previously, a strategic imperative to make American Express an essential part of customers’ digital lives has become embedded in the company’s operations. The company also has an Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) strategy with three pillars: promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DE&I) to foster a diverse, equitable, and inclusive workforce and society; advancing climate solutions by enhancing operations to meet customer and community needs in a low-carbon future; and building financial confidence by offering responsible, secure, and transparent products and services to help individuals and businesses achieve financial resilience. The company emphasizes a culture built on supportive relationships and inclusivity, where colleagues feel welcome, heard, and supported in their growth. This culture is guided by the Blue Box Values: We Do What's Right, We Embrace Diversity, We Back Our Customers, We Stand for Equity and Inclusion, We Make It Great, We Win as a Team, We Respect People, and We Support Communities. As of December 31, 2022, American Express employed approximately 77,300 colleagues, with about 26,000 in the United States and 51,300 outside the United States. The company added colleagues in 2022 to support business growth. To attract and retain top talent, it offers competitive compensation and leading benefits and invests in programs such as on-the-job learning tools, cross-border assignments, career coaching, mentoring, rotation opportunities, virtual learning, and formal classroom instruction. The health and wellness of colleagues is a priority, with a holistic approach addressing physical, financial, and mental well-being. In 2022, the company launched Amex Flex, allowing colleagues to work in the office, at home, or in a hybrid model based on role and business needs, to broaden the talent pool and improve retention. An annual Colleague Experience Survey showed that 92 percent of participating colleagues would recommend American Express as a great place to work. The 2022 company scorecard included talent retention, colleague engagement, and diversity representation goals. As of December 31, 2022, women made up 53.7 percent of the global workforce, and in the U.S. workforce, Asian, Black/African American, and Hispanic/Latinx colleagues represented 18.7 percent, 17.9 percent, and 14.2 percent, respectively, based on preliminary 2022 U.S. EEO-1 data. Fifty-two percent of the Executive Committee were women or from diverse racial and ethnic backgrounds (based on self-identified characteristics). The company regularly reviews compensation practices to ensure fairness across genders globally and across races and ethnicities in the U.S., considering factors such as role, level, tenure, performance, and geography. After adjustments for inconsistencies, the company maintained 100 percent pay equity in 2022 globally for genders and across races and ethnicities in the U.S. The executive officers as of February 10, 2023, are listed in alphabetical order, with no family relationships among them and no appointments based on arrangements with others. Each officer serves until the next annual election or until a successor is elected and qualified. The officers include Douglas E. Buckminster (62), Vice Chairman since April 2021; Jeffrey C. Squeri (63), Chairman and Chief Executive Officer since February 2018; and Anré Williams (57), Group President, Enterprise Services since April 2021. American Express competes globally in the payments industry with card networks, issuers, acquirers, paper-based transactions, bank transfers, and emerging alternative payment and financing mechanisms such as digital wallets, open banking, buy now, pay later products, real-time settlement systems, financial technology companies, digital currencies, blockchain, prepaid systems, and gift cards. As a card issuer, it competes with financial institutions offering general-purpose credit and debit cards, private label card issuers, mobile wallet providers, and companies offering credit. It faces intense competition in the premium segment and for cobrand relationships, as well as for partners and differentiated offerings like airport lounge access. The company competes with other global card networks, including China UnionPay, Visa, Mastercard, JCB, Discover, and Diners Club International (owned by Discover), and is the fourth largest general-purpose card network globally by purchase volume. Other companies, including merchant acquirers, processors, and digital platforms like Alipay, PayPal, and Venmo, as well as regional networks like the National Payments Corporation of India, perform similar activities. Key competitive factors include product and service features, brand reputation, customer spending and credit performance, merchant acceptance, value proposition attractiveness, availability of alternative payment and financing options, marketing effectiveness, innovation speed, expense management tools, and data capabilities, particularly for business customers, and the security of cardholder, merchant, and network partner information. The rapid growth of alternative payment mechanisms, including financial services integration and closed-loop loyalty features, presents ongoing competitive challenges. Additionally, the company faces significant government regulation and supervision worldwide, with substantial compliance costs, and regulatory scrutiny, high expectations, and unpredictable enforcement environments.

Results may materially suffer due to substantial and increasingly intense global competition in the payments industry, as discussed in the “Risk Factors” section, and the business is subject to comprehensive government regulation and supervision, which could materially adversely affect operations and financial condition. Legal proceedings related to provisions in merchant contracts—such as non-discrimination and honor-all-cards—could have a material adverse effect on the business, leading to additional litigation or arbitrations, changes to merchant agreements or business practices, substantial monetary damages, and reputational harm. The Company, TRS, and its U.S. bank subsidiary, American Express National Bank (AENB), are subject to extensive federal and state banking laws, regulations, and policies, including oversight by the Federal Reserve, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). Both the Company and TRS are consolidatedly supervised by the Federal Reserve, with AENB under OCC supervision. The Company and TRS have elected financial holding company status, which allows broader financial activities, but must maintain eligibility requirements, including being “well capitalized” and “well managed,” and AENB receiving a “satisfactory” CRA rating. The Company and its subsidiaries are prohibited from engaging in practices deemed unsafe or unsound by regulators, who have discretion in determining safe and sound operations. Acquisitions and investments are subject to regulatory review and approval by the Federal Reserve and OCC, with broad discretion in evaluations. The Company is subject to U.S. federal bank regulatory rules that categorize bank holding companies based on risk indicators, placing the Company in Category IV. As a Category IV firm, it is not subject to advanced approaches capital requirements and must maintain minimum capital ratios of 4.5% CET1, 6.0% Tier 1, and 8.0% Total capital to risk-weighted assets. The Company is subject to a dynamic stress capital buffer (SCB) of 2.5% CET1 capital, effective from October 1 each year, increasing the effective minimum ratios to 7.0% CET1, 8.5% Tier 1, and 10.5% Total capital. AENB is subject to a static 2.5% capital conservation buffer. The Company must maintain a leverage ratio of at least 4.0%. Liquidity requirements under the Federal Reserve’s enhanced prudential standards include a liquidity buffer and a minimum liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), but Category IV firms with less than $50 billion in weighted short-term wholesale funding, like the Company, are not subject to specific LCR or net stable funding ratio (NSFR) requirements. The Company participates in supervisory stress testing every other year, with the most recent test in 2022, and must submit an annual capital plan by April 5. The SCB based on stress tests is recalculated every other year, and the firm may elect to participate in an “off year” to receive an updated SCB. Capital distributions, including dividends and share repurchases, are limited if capital ratios fall below minimums or if the capital plan is resubmitted. AENB’s ability to pay dividends to TRS is restricted by law and requires approval from the OCC if not paid from recent earnings or if it would breach capital adequacy. The Federal Deposit Insurance Act (FDIA) imposes progressive restrictions on institutions based on capital categories, with AENB required to maintain CET1, Tier 1, Total capital, and Tier 1 leverage ratios of at least 6.5%, 8.0%, 10.0%, and 5.0%, respectively, to be considered “well capitalized.” AENB may be prohibited from accepting brokered deposits or offering interest rates above prevailing market rates unless well capitalized or adequately capitalized with a waiver. The Company is not required to submit a holding company resolution plan, but AENB must submit a resolution plan every three years, with the most recent submission in December 2022. The Company could become subject to the Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA), under which the Treasury Secretary may appoint the FDIC as receiver to liquidate a systemically important institution in the event of default and systemic risk, with significant differences from the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, including the FDIC’s authority to disregard creditor claim priorities.

AENB is required to prepare and submit a separate resolution plan to the FDIC to enable the FDIC, as receiver, to effectively resolve the institution under the FDIA in the event of failure. Under the FDIC’s rule and its June 2021 statement, insured depository institutions with $100 billion or more in assets—such as AENB—are required to submit resolution plans on a three-year cycle, and AENB submitted its most recent resolution plan in December 2022 as required. The Company could become subject to the Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA), under which the Treasury Secretary may appoint the FDIC as receiver to liquidate a systemically important financial institution if the Company is in danger of default and poses a systemic risk to U.S. financial stability. Under the OLA, the FDIC has broad powers as receiver, including the ability to disregard the strict priority of creditor claims in limited circumstances, use an administrative claims procedure instead of judicial proceedings, and transfer claims to a “bridge” entity. The FDIC has developed a “single point of entry” (SPOE) strategy under OLA, whereby the FDIC would transfer AENB’s assets—including shares of its operating subsidiaries—and potentially limited liabilities to a “bridge” holding company; use the failed company’s resources to recapitalize its subsidiaries; and satisfy unsecured creditor claims and other claimants by delivering securities from new financial companies emerging from the bridge entity. Under this strategy, management of the failed holding company would be replaced, and shareholders and creditors would bear the losses. If the FDIC is appointed conservator or receiver of AENB, it has the power to transfer any of AENB’s assets or liabilities to a new obligor without creditor approval, enforce contractual terms, or repudiate or disaffirm contracts or leases deemed burdensome by the FDIC. Additionally, claims of U.S. deposit holders and certain administrative expenses of the FDIC would be prioritized over other general unsecured claims, including those of debt holders and depositors in non-U.S. offices, meaning such non-U.S. depositors could receive substantially less or nothing compared to U.S. office depositors. The Company is required to act as a source of financial and managerial strength to its U.S. bank subsidiary, AENB, and may be required to commit capital or financial resources to support AENB even when it would otherwise not do so. Capital loans to AENB are subordinate to deposits and certain other indebtedness of AENB, and in the event of the Company’s bankruptcy, any commitment to a federal banking regulator to maintain AENB’s capital would be assumed by the bankruptcy trustee and given priority of payment. Certain transactions between AENB and its affiliates—including the Company, TRS, and their subsidiaries—are subject to quantitative and qualitative limitations, collateral requirements, and other restrictions under statute and regulation and must generally be made on an arm’s-length basis. AENB accepts deposits insured by the FDIC up to applicable limits, and the FDIC may terminate such insurance if AENB engages in unsafe or unsound practices, is in an unsafe or unsound condition, or violates applicable laws, regulations, rules, orders, or conditions. There is no known practice, condition, or violation at AENB that would lead to termination of deposit insurance. The FDIC’s deposit insurance fund is funded by assessments on insured institutions, including AENB, which are subject to adjustment by the FDIC. AENB is subject to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), which imposes affirmative, ongoing obligations to meet the credit needs of local communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with safe and sound operations. In May 2022, federal banking agencies issued a joint notice of proposed rulemaking proposing revisions to CRA regulations, including changes to assessment areas, evaluation frameworks, performance standards, definitions of community development activities, and data collection and reporting. The U.S. banking agencies have increased their focus on climate risk-related supervision; on December 16, 2021, the OCC issued for public comment proposed “Principles for Climate-Related Financial Risk Management for Large Banks,” which apply to OCC-regulated institutions with over $100 billion in total consolidated assets, such as AENB, and cover governance, policies, strategic planning, risk management, data and reporting, and scenario analysis. The principles also offer guidance on incorporating climate risks into traditional risk categories. On March 30, 2022, and December 2, 2022, the FDIC and the Federal Reserve, respectively, issued for public comment similar draft principles for financial institutions with over $100 billion in assets under their supervision, including the Company. It is too early to determine what regulations or policies may be adopted or applied, and the potential impact on the Company and AENB remains uncertain. The Company’s consumer-oriented activities are regulated in the U.S. and internationally; in the U.S., the CFPB supervises and examines marketing, sale, and servicing of consumer financial products and enforces federal consumer financial laws, including preventing “unfair, deceptive, or abusive” practices, collecting fines, requiring restitution, engaging in consumer education, tracking complaints, requesting data, and promoting access to underserved consumers. U.S. state laws also impose significant consumer credit protection, disclosure, and other requirements, some of which are more stringent than federal laws. Federal law also regulates abusive debt collection practices, which can affect the Company’s ability to collect amounts owed and subject it to regulatory scrutiny. On February 1, 2023, the CFPB issued a proposed rule to lower the safe harbor amount for late fees considered “reasonable and proportional” to costs incurred by credit card issuers, eliminate annual inflation adjustments, and prohibit late fees above 25% of the consumer’s required minimum payment; if adopted, this rule is not expected to become effective before 2024. The Company is also subject to “money transmitter” or “sale of check” laws in most U.S. states, unclaimed and abandoned property laws requiring payment of face amounts of uncashed Travelers Cheques or unredeemed prepaid cards after a specified period, and insurance laws in the U.S. and other countries where it offers insurance services. Outside the U.S., regulators focus on consumer protection (e.g., EU, UK, Canada) and responsible lending (e.g., Australia, Mexico, New Zealand, Singapore), with increasing emphasis on customer outcomes rather than compliance. Regulators are placing greater emphasis on firms’ compliance, risk, and control frameworks, particularly in systems and controls for identifying and resolving issues. In various jurisdictions, legislators and regulators have focused on card network operations, including enforcement actions, legislation, and regulations affecting interchange fees, merchant card acceptance, and pricing, and establishing ongoing oversight of payment systems. Regulation of interchange fees has negatively impacted and may continue to negatively impact the Company’s discount revenue due to downward pressure on merchant discount rates from reduced competitor pricing under interchange fee caps. The Company has exited its network businesses in the EU and Australia due to regulation in those jurisdictions. There is uncertainty regarding when or how interchange fee caps and other provisions of EU payments legislation might apply in cobrand partnerships and agent arrangements in the EU, and differing regulatory interpretations could lead to regulatory action, penalties, or the loss of existing cobrand and agent relationships. In certain EU Member States and Australia, merchants are permitted by law to surcharge card purchases. In the U.S., laws prohibiting surcharging have been overturned, and some states have passed or are considering surcharging laws. Effective October 6, 2022, merchants in Canada (excluding Quebec) are permitted to surcharge credit card purchases up to a maximum of 2.4%, resulting from a litigation settlement with Visa and Mastercard. Surcharging is an adverse customer experience and could materially harm the Company, especially if it disproportionately affects credit card usage or card usage generally, its Card Members, or its business. Other steering or differential acceptance practices permitted by regulation in some jurisdictions could also have a material adverse effect. In some countries, governments require international card networks to be locally licensed or to localize operations; for example, India’s Reserve Bank of India, under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, mandated local storage of payment data and imposed restrictions on American Express Banking Corp. in 2021, which were lifted in August 2022 after significant investment in technology, infrastructure, and resources to comply. The development and enforcement of such laws may adversely affect the Company’s ability to compete and maintain its global network. Regulatory and legislative activity in privacy, data protection, data governance, information, and cyber security continues to increase worldwide. The Company has established and maintains policies and a governance framework to comply with applicable laws and meet evolving customer and industry expectations. Regulators are increasingly focused on ensuring that privacy, data protection, cyber security policies and practices adequately inform customers about data collection, use, sharing, and security, provide them with choices, and appropriately safeguard personal information and account access. Regulators also emphasize data management, resiliency, business continuity, and third-party risk management. In the U.S., certain businesses are subject to the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA) and its regulations, which limit sharing of consumers’ nonpublic personal information with nonaffiliated third parties and require a written comprehensive information security program appropriate to the business size, complexity, and sensitivity of customer data. The Company has expanded privacy rights for California residents under the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 and the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020. Various U.S. regulators, states, and territories are considering or have adopted privacy or cyber security laws that may be more stringent or expansive than federal requirements. The Company is also subject to privacy, data protection, data governance, and cyber security laws in other countries, including the EU, Australia, Canada, China, Japan, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Singapore, Thailand, and the UK, some of which are more stringent or expansive than U.S. laws and may conflict with each other. Some jurisdictions impose onerous requirements for transferring personal data to other jurisdictions, while others require in-country data processing or storage. Compliance increases technology, administrative, and other costs, limits the ability to optimize closed-loop data, and may require local technology services. Some laws also require broader access to data and intellectual property by foreign governments or third parties. Data breach and operational outage notification laws, as well as regulatory activities promoting such notifications and resiliency, business continuity, and third-party risk management, are becoming more prevalent in jurisdictions outside the U.S. In Europe, the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) imposes legal and compliance obligations on companies processing personal data of individuals in the EU, regardless of location, with potential fines up to 4% of total worldwide annual revenue. The GDPR requires prompt notification of data breaches to affected individuals and supervisory authorities. The UK GDPR mirrors the GDPR’s compliance requirements and fine structure. In October 2022, an Executive Order, together with U.S. Department of Justice regulations, was signed to implement a new data privacy framework for cross-border transfers of EU personal data to the U.S. The Company is also subject to significant supervision and an increasingly stringent enforcement environment regarding compliance with anti-money laundering (AML), countering the financing of terrorism (CFT), economic sanctions, and anti-corruption laws. Failure to maintain adequate AML/CFT, sanctions, and anti-corruption programs and procedures could result in material financial, legal, and reputational consequences. In the U.S., AML/CFT requirements primarily stem from the Currency and Foreign Transactions Reporting Act and regulations issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury (Bank Secrecy Act), as amended by the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001. The Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AMLA), enacted in January 2021, amended the Bank Secrecy Act and aims to comprehensively reform and modernize U.S. AML/CFT laws, with many statutory provisions requiring additional rulemakings, reports, and measures, the effects of which are not yet known. In Europe, AML/CFT requirements are largely derived from countries transposing the 5th and 6th EU Anti-Money Laundering Directives (and earlier directives) into local laws.

We are subject to a significant number of anti-money laundering and counterfinancing of terrorism (AML/CFT) laws and regulations globally. In the United States, the majority of AML/CFT requirements stem from the Currency and Foreign Transactions Reporting Act and the regulations issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, collectively known as the Bank Secrecy Act, as amended by the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001. The Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AMLA), enacted in January 2021, amended the Bank Secrecy Act and aims to comprehensively reform and modernize U.S. AML/CFT laws. Many of its statutory provisions will require additional rulemakings, reports, and other measures, the effects of which are not yet known. In Europe, AML/CFT requirements arise primarily from countries transposing the 5th and 6th EU Anti-Money Laundering Directives (and earlier directives) into local laws and regulations. Numerous other countries, including Argentina, Australia, Canada, India, Mexico, New Zealand, and Russia, have enacted or proposed new or enhanced AML/CFT legislation applicable to American Express. These laws and regulations require us to establish AML/CFT programs that meet certain standards, including expanded reporting—particularly on suspicious transactions—and enhanced information gathering and recordkeeping. Our AML/CFT programs have faced heightened scrutiny in some countries, including certain EU Member States. Any errors, failures, or delays in complying with AML/CFT laws, perceived deficiencies in our programs, or an association of our business with money laundering, terrorist financing, tax fraud, or other illicit activity can lead to significant supervisory, criminal, and civil proceedings and lawsuits, resulting in substantial penalties, forfeiture of assets, loss of licenses, restrictions on business activities, or other enforcement actions. We are also subject to economic sanctions imposed by national governments and international bodies such as the United Nations and the EU, targeting individuals, entities, vessels, governments, and countries that threaten their interests or violate international norms. These sanctions are used to advance foreign policy goals such as conflict resolution, counterterrorism, counternarcotics, and promotion of democracy and human rights. Failure to comply can result in serious legal and reputational consequences, including criminal penalties. The United States has imposed sanctions affecting transactions with designated foreign countries, nationals, and others, prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging with individuals or entities listed as “Specially Designated Nationals” (such as terrorists and narcotics traffickers) without a license or authorization. These prohibitions are administered by the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which prohibits financial transactions with such entities, requires the blocking of assets in which they have an interest, and bans transfers of property subject to U.S. jurisdiction. Blocked assets, such as property or bank deposits, cannot be paid out, withdrawn, set off, or transferred without an OFAC license. We maintain a global sanctions compliance program to meet the requirements of applicable sanctions regimes. We are also subject to complex anti-corruption laws, including the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), the UK Bribery Act, and other laws that prohibit improper payments. The FCPA makes it illegal to offer or provide anything of value to foreign government officials, political parties, or political party officials to obtain or retain business or an improper advantage. It also requires strict compliance with accounting and internal controls. The UK Bribery Act prohibits commercial bribery and receipt of bribes and makes it a corporate offense to fail to prevent bribery by an associated person, in addition to prohibiting improper payments to foreign government officials. Failure by us or our colleagues, contractors, or agents to comply with the FCPA, the UK Bribery Act, or similar laws can result in investigations, prosecutions, and potentially severe criminal and civil penalties. Our compensation practices are overseen by the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). Federal banking regulators’ guidance on sound incentive compensation practices outlines three key principles: (1) incentives should appropriately balance risk and financial results without encouraging imprudent risk-taking, (2) incentive plans must be compatible with effective internal controls and risk management, and (3) they must be supported by strong corporate governance, including active and effective oversight by the board of directors. Deficiencies in our compensation practices identified by regulators may be incorporated into our supervisory ratings, affecting our ability to make acquisitions or perform other actions. Enforcement actions may be taken if our incentive compensation arrangements or related risk-management or governance processes are found to pose a risk to our safety and soundness and we have not taken prompt and effective corrective measures. The Dodd-Frank Act requires U.S. financial regulators, including the Federal Reserve and the SEC, to adopt rules on incentive-based payment arrangements for entities with at least $1 billion in total assets. In 2016, the federal banking regulators, the SEC, the Federal Housing Finance Agency, and the National Credit Union Administration proposed revised rules on incentive-based compensation practices, which have not yet been finalized. If adopted in a form similar to the proposal, these rules would impose limitations on how we structure compensation for our colleagues, potentially harming our ability to hire, retain, and motivate key personnel. In October 2022, the SEC adopted a new rule requiring national securities exchanges to mandate policies that require the recovery of excess incentive-based compensation paid to current or former executive officers in the case of a restatement of previously issued financial statements, and require listed issuers to disclose any recovery analysis triggered by such restatements. Our business as a whole has not experienced significant seasonal fluctuations, although network volumes are moderately higher in the fourth quarter than in other quarters, leading to moderately higher Card Member loans and receivables during that period. The average discount rate tends to be slightly lower in the fourth quarter due to a higher level of retail-related billed business. Our business is subject to the effects of geopolitical conditions, weather, natural disasters, and other catastrophic events. Geopolitical instability, terrorist attacks, severe weather, pandemics, cybersecurity incidents, operational disruptions, and other catastrophic events can have a material adverse effect on our business. Political and social conditions, including actions that disrupt geopolitical stability, fiscal and monetary policies (such as developments related to the U.S. federal debt ceiling), trade wars and tariffs, labor shortages, government shutdowns, regional or domestic hostilities, economic sanctions, and the prospect or occurrence of broader conflicts can negatively affect our business, operations, partners, consumer and business spending, including travel patterns and business investment, and demand for credit. Because we derive a portion of our revenues from travel-related spending, our business is sensitive to travel safety concerns, limitations on travel and mobility, and health-related risks. Disruptions in air travel and other forms of travel can result in claims under travel protection products we offer. The COVID-19 pandemic had and continues to have widespread, rapidly evolving, and unpredictable impacts on global society, economies, financial markets, and consumer and business spending. The pandemic and resulting containment measures adversely impacted a significant portion of our network volumes. The global macroeconomic outlook remains uncertain due to factors such as new virus variants, labor market impacts, supply chain disruptions, and inflation, and the pandemic’s effects may persist even as the pandemic subsides. The extent to which our business and results of operations could continue to be adversely affected by lingering pandemic impacts depends on evolving factors such as the spread and severity of the virus, the imposition or concern about further containment measures, the availability and effectiveness of treatments and vaccines, the economic, inflationary, and consumer confidence impacts, the end of forbearance and government support programs, ongoing business stress from operational changes and staffing issues, and the resumption of normal operating conditions and customer behaviors. Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, we suspended all business operations in Russia and Belarus, and this conflict has led to economic uncertainty and market disruptions, including heightened energy prices, and the imposition of financial and economic sanctions and export controls to constrain Russia. The broader consequences remain uncertain and may include further sanctions, regional instability, geopolitical shifts, increased sophistication of cyberattacks, potential retaliatory actions by customers or the Russian government against companies like us, heightened regulatory scrutiny related to sanctions compliance, increased inflation, further fluctuations in commodity and energy prices, decreases in global travel, further supply chain disruptions, reduced availability of certain natural resources, and other adverse macroeconomic effects. Hurricanes and other natural disasters have impacted spending and credit performance in affected areas. Future disasters or catastrophic events and their impact on industries or the overall economy could negatively affect our business, results of operations, and infrastructure, including our technology and systems. Climate change may exacerbate these threats, including the frequency and severity of weather-related events. Card Members in California, New York, Florida, Texas, Georgia, and New Jersey account for a significant portion of U.S. consumer and small business billed business and Card Member loans, and our results of operations could be impacted by events or conditions that disproportionately or specifically affect one or more of these states. Our operating results may materially suffer due to substantial and increasingly intense competition in the global payments industry. The payments industry is highly competitive, and we compete with card networks, issuers, acquirers, paper-based transactions (such as cash and checks), bank transfer models (such as wire transfers and ACH), and evolving alternative payment and financing providers. If we fail to differentiate ourselves, develop compelling value propositions for customers, or effectively grow in areas such as mobile and online payments and emerging technologies, we may not compete effectively. We believe Visa and Mastercard are larger than we are in most countries based on purchase volume, and as a result, card issuers and acquirers on those networks may benefit from their dominant position, scale, resources, marketing, and pricing. Our business may also be negatively affected if we are unable to continue increasing merchant acceptance—including by merchants that accept cards on Visa and Mastercard networks—or if our Card Members do not experience welcome acceptance of our cards. Some of our competitors have greater financial and other resources than we do and may offer richer value propositions, a wider range of programs and services, or use more effective strategies to acquire and retain customers, capture a greater share of spending and borrowings, develop more attractive cobrand cards and partner programs, and maintain greater merchant acceptance. Government actions or initiatives may also provide competitors with increased competitive advantages and create new competitors, including government entities. We may not be able to compete effectively against these threats or respond as effectively as our competitors to changes in consumer spending and borrowing habits. Costs such as Card Member rewards and services expenses could continue to rise as we evolve our value propositions in response to increased competition. Spending on our cards could continue to be impacted by increasing consumer use of credit and debit cards issued on other networks and the adoption of alternative payment mechanisms, systems, and products. The fragmentation of customer spending to take advantage of different merchant or card incentives or for convenience with technological solutions may continue to increase. Revolving credit balances on our cards could also be affected by alternative financing providers, such as point-of-sale lenders and buy now, pay later products. To the extent other payment and financing mechanisms, systems, and products continue to expand successfully, our discount revenues from Card Member spending and our net interest income from Card Member borrowing could be negatively impacted. Companies that control access to consumer and merchant payment choices at the point of sale or through digital wallets, commerce experiences, mobile applications, or other technologies could choose not to accept, suppress, or degrade the use of our products or could restrict our access to customer data. Such companies could also require payments from us to participate in digital wallets, experiences, or applications or negotiate incentives or pricing concessions, which could impact our profitability on transactions. The competitive value of our closed-loop data and demand for our products and services may also decline as traditional and non-traditional competitors use new data sources and technologies to derive similar insights, and as certain regulations—such as open banking initiatives—may disintermediate existing financial services providers, steer customers away from our products and services, or reduce our attractiveness to partners. To the extent we expand into or further grow in new business areas and geographic regions, such as mainland China, we will face competitors with more experience and more established relationships with relevant customers, regulators, and industry participants, which could adversely affect our ability to compete. Laws and business practices that favor local competitors, require card transactions to be routed over domestic networks, or prohibit or limit foreign ownership of certain businesses could limit our growth in international regions. We may face additional compliance and regulatory challenges in these areas.

Through digital wallets, commerce-related experiences, mobile applications, or other technologies, companies could choose not to accept, suppress, or degrade the use of our products, restrict our access to customer and transaction data, or require payments from us to participate, which could negatively impact our profitability. The competitive value of our closed-loop data and demand for our products and services may decline as traditional and non-traditional competitors leverage alternative data sources and technologies to gain similar insights, and due to regulations like open banking, which may disintermediate financial services providers, steer customers away from our offerings, or reduce our appeal to partners. As we expand into new business areas or geographic regions—such as mainland China—we will face competitors with greater experience and established customer, regulatory, and industry relationships, which could hinder our competitiveness. Local laws and business practices that favor domestic competitors, require card transactions to be routed over domestic networks, or prohibit or limit foreign ownership could restrict our growth in international markets. Expanding into new areas increases compliance and regulatory risks, requiring more expense, time, and resources to meet regulatory requirements than our competitors, especially if they are not regulated financial institutions. Many of our competitors operate under less stringent legislative and regulatory regimes, have lower cost structures, and more agile business models, putting us at a disadvantage, particularly where laws restrict certain transactions, regulate business practices, or increase our costs. We face intense competition for partner relationships, which could lead to loss or renegotiation of agreements, materially affecting our business and operations. We have partnered with Delta, Marriott, Hilton, British Airways, and many other global businesses to offer cobranded cards and benefits through our Membership Rewards program. All cobrand portfolios collectively accounted for approximately 18 percent of our worldwide network volumes as of December 31, 2022, and card member loans related to these portfolios accounted for about 36 percent of our worldwide card member loans at that date. Cobrand arrangements typically last between five and ten years and terminate at the end of the term unless renewed or extended, or early due to default. We face the risk of losing partner relationships, even after significant investment, and may choose not to renew certain arrangements. Termination of cobrand partnerships could lead to a decline in network volumes and increased card member attrition, and some arrangements allow the cobrand partner to purchase or designate a third party to purchase the loans generated, resulting in loss of card accounts and a significant reduction in outstanding card member loans. We regularly seek to extend or renew these arrangements, but face risks of renegotiating on less favorable terms or being unable to secure acceptable terms due to rising competition. We make payments to cobrand partners based on Card Member spending, rewards earned, and in some cases, the number of accounts acquired and retained, with payments increasing, particularly in the U.S., due to heightened competition. Loss of exclusivity, complete termination of partnerships—such as the end of the relationship with Costco in the U.S. in 2016 or American Airlines’ withdrawal from the Airport Club Access program in 2014—or renegotiation with worse terms could materially harm our business. Publicity surrounding such losses could damage our reputation, making it harder to attract and retain card members and merchants and weakening our negotiating power with current and prospective partners. Business partner arrangements represent a significant portion of our operations, exposing us to risks such as reputational issues, business slowdowns, bankruptcies, liquidations, restructurings, and consolidations, as well as potential obligations to make payments upon performance shortfalls or revenue declines. Our success is closely tied to our partners’ performance, from customer acquisition to cobranding, rewards programs, and B2B supplier payments. If partners fail to promote or support our products, experience operational disruptions, reputational issues, or lose consumer confidence, our business could be materially harmed. We also face risks of being required to make or accelerate payments to partners upon triggering events, which could negatively affect our financial condition. We have previously and may in the future pre-purchase loyalty points from cobrand partners, whose value could decline if the partners cease operations or if the points become less desirable. We could also be materially impacted if we are obligated or choose to reimburse card members for products or services from merchants that have ceased operations or stopped accepting our cards. For example, in the airline industry, we face credit risk when card members purchase tickets that are not delivered or flown; if we cannot recover the amount from the airline, we may bear the loss. At December 31, 2022, our best estimate of the maximum amount of billed business for undelivered purchases was $31.1 billion, assuming all such merchants cease operations and all claims are made in full; this is not indicative of actual losses, and no significant losses have been experienced to date, though historical experience may not reflect current conditions. We face continued competitive pressure that may reduce the prices we charge for card acceptance and increase the risk of losing merchant relationships, which could harm our business. Competitors relying on non-discount revenue or with lower costs offer more attractive pricing, and merchants, business partners, and third-party acquirers can negotiate incentives, pricing concessions, or favorable terms as a condition for accepting our cards or becoming partners. As merchants grow—such as large tech companies—we may need to increase incentives or concessions. We also face the risk of losing key merchant relationships, which could negatively impact network volumes, card member retention, and attraction. Our average merchant discount rate has been affected by regulatory changes in certain international markets and may be further impacted by pricing regulations. We have experienced erosion of this rate as merchant acceptance grows, and we may not succeed in expanding acceptance or offsetting rate declines with volume growth at new merchants. The evolving regulatory environment and alternative payment models from non-traditional players could challenge our traditional payment model and reduce our average merchant discount rate. Large merchants, including tech companies, are investing in proprietary mobile wallets and payment solutions using traditional and new technologies. If these solutions gain broad consumer adoption, they could reduce our average merchant discount rate and network volumes. A key focus is delivering greater and differentiated value to merchants; failure to do so could harm our discount revenue and financial results. We may not succeed in maintaining merchant discount rates or offsetting declining rates, which could materially and adversely affect our revenues, profitability, and ability to invest in innovation and value-added services. Surcharging or steering by merchants could materially harm our business. In countries like Australia, certain EU Member States, and some U.S. states, merchants are legally permitted to surcharge card purchases, and in some jurisdictions, such as Canada, surcharging is permitted due to litigation settlements. In these areas, we have observed surcharging on American Express cards, sometimes exceeding that of Visa or Mastercard or not applying to those cards at all—known as differential surcharging—despite similar acceptance costs. Some merchants accept our cards but inform customers they prefer other payment types, which could increase with the availability of debit cards on the American Express network. Our Card Members value the ability to use their cards freely, and we enforce non-discrimination and honor-all-cards provisions in merchant contracts, subject to local laws. We increasingly rely on merchant acquirers, aggregators, and processors to manage merchant relationships, but they may have interests inconsistent with ours. New products like debit cards could fail to gain market acceptance, leading to reduced cards-in-force, coverage, and transaction volumes due to surcharging, steering, or other forms of discrimination, with impacts varying by industry, surcharge structure, implementation ease, charge size, and whether the discrimination applies to credit, debit, or specific products. Such discrimination could materially harm our business, financial condition, and results. We may not succeed in promoting card usage through marketing, merchant acceptance, or rewards, or in controlling the costs of these investments, which could materially affect profitability. Revenue growth depends on increased consumer and business spending, growing loan balances, and fee revenue. We are investing in growth initiatives to attract new card members, retain existing ones, and capture a larger share of customer spending and borrowing. There is no guarantee these investments will remain effective as consumer and business behaviors evolve. If we introduce products offering short-term incentives instead of long-term loyalty, card member attrition and costs could rise. Increased spending depends on continued merchant acceptance; if we fail to grow acceptance or if merchants stop accepting American Express cards, our business could suffer. Expanding services, adding acquisition channels, or forming or renewing partnerships may incur higher costs, fail to resonate with customers, reduce our average discount rate, or dilute our brand. Through our Membership Rewards program and other benefits, we provide value to card members; however, significant changes or failures in estimating actual redemptions and associated costs could harm profitability. We rely on third parties for redemption options, with Amazon and Delta being our two largest partners; if we cannot continue offering these options, the program’s value may decline. Many credit card issuers have introduced similar or more attractive rewards and cobrand programs, and our inability to differentiate our offerings could materially harm us. We may not be able to cost-effectively manage and expand card member benefits, including containing growth in marketing, promotion, rewards, and service expenses. If these costs exceed expectations, we will need to offset the impact by increasing fee-based revenues, reducing operating expenses, or cutting investments, which may not be feasible in the current competitive and regulatory environment. Inflation, colleague retention and recruitment, supply chain issues, and material shortages—such as chips for our cards—could require reductions in other areas of investment. Our brand and reputation are key assets, and our ability to attract and retain card members and corporate clients depends on external perceptions of our service quality, trustworthiness, business practices, privacy, data protection, management, workplace culture, financial health, response to political and social issues, or catastrophic events—including the COVID-19 pandemic and natural disasters. Negative perceptions—whether from isolated incidents or alleged misconduct—could erode trust and damage our reputation among existing and potential customers, merchants, and partners, making it difficult to attract or retain them. Negative public opinion can arise from card practices, regulatory compliance, customer information use, employee conduct, policy engagement—including activities of the American Express Company Political Action Committee—and from regulatory or third-party actions. Social media discussions about such matters can rapidly and widely harm our brand. Our brand and reputation may also be harmed by actions taken by third parties outside our control.
